cves.summary:
**Ecosystem / package:** Go — `github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark` (the `kubeshark`
CLI, `kubeshark mcp` subcommand)
**Affected component:** `cmd/mcpRunner.go`, MCP tool `start_kubeshark`
**Affected versions:** `>= v53.1.0`, `< v53.4.0` (the flaw shipped with the MCP
command's first release; v53.3.0 was the last affected release)
**Patched version:** `v53.4.0`
**Credit:** novice-22 (Urim), via private coordinated disclosure.

## Summary
The `start_kubeshark` MCP tool builds a `kubeshark tap` command by appending the
caller-supplied `pod_regex` as a bare positional argument, with no `--`
end-of-options separator. Because `tap` is a cobra command, a `pod_regex` that
begins with `-`/`--set=` is parsed as a **flag**, not as the pod regex. An
attacker who can influence the tool arguments (e.g. indirect prompt injection
against an agent driving `kubeshark mcp --allow-destructive`) can inject
arbitrary `--set` Helm value overrides — notably `tap.docker.registry` /
`tap.docker.tag` — redirecting the deployed worker/hub/front images to an
attacker-controlled registry. The worker DaemonSet runs privileged with
`hostNetwork` and the host filesystem mounted, so an attacker image yields node
and cluster-admin compromise.

## Introduced in
Commit `0bbbb473` — "[1] Add MCP (Model Context Protocol) server command
(#1832)", 2026-02-06 — first released in **v53.1.0** (`v53.1.0~23`). The
`pod_regex` argument has been appended as a bare positional since the tool's
introduction; there is no regression window, every MCP-capable release is
affected.

## Details
In `callStartKubeshark` (`cmd/mcpRunner.go`), the command was built as
`["tap", <pod_regex>, "-n", …, "--set", …, "--set", "headless=true"]` with
`pod_regex` inserted as a raw element. cobra parses flags positionally-agnostic
and there was no `--` guard, so `pod_regex="--set=tap.docker.registry=…,tap.docker.tag=…"`
became a real `--set`. The tool is only registered when
`kubeshark mcp --allow-destructive` is set.

## Proof of concept (reporter, abridged)
Driving `kubeshark mcp --allow-destructive`: `start_kubeshark` with
`pod_regex="--set=tap.docker.registry=<attacker>,tap.docker.tag=<tag>"` caused
the CLI to construct `kubeshark tap --set=… --set headless=true`, deploying an
attacker image. The image ran as root inside the privileged worker container and
read the host's cluster-admin kubeconfigs
(`/etc/kubernetes/super-admin.conf`, `admin.conf`, `pki/`) — i.e. cluster-admin
takeover from a single `pod_regex` value.

## Impact
Full Kubernetes cluster compromise (cluster-admin) from a single injected tool
argument, when the operator runs the MCP server with `--allow-destructive`.

## Severity rationale
Kubeshark scores this **7.2 High**, down from the reporter's 8.3, on two metrics. The
impact half of the vector (`S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H`) is unchanged — cluster-admin
takeover is real and Kubeshark does not contest it.

- **`AV:N` → `AV:L`.** `kubeshark mcp` is a local stdio MCP server with no
  network listener. The attacker's payload reaches it as content an agent
  running on that host ingested and replayed into a local tool call. The
  poisoned content may have travelled over a network, but the exploited
  interface is local.
- **`PR:N` → `PR:H`.** Two administrative preconditions must already hold on the
  target host: the operator must have started the MCP server with the explicit,
  non-default `--allow-destructive` flag (without it `start_kubeshark` is not
  registered at all), and that host must already hold a kubeconfig with
  permission to deploy the privileged Kubeshark DaemonSet. The attacker is
  borrowing an existing high-privilege context, not gaining one.

Kubeshark kept **`AC:H`** (the injection must land in content the agent ingests, and
the attacker must stand up a malicious registry/image), **`UI:R`** (an operator
must be actively driving the agent), and **`S:C`** (the compromise crosses from
the CLI's authorization scope into the Kubernetes cluster — this is what keeps
the score in the High band).

## Patches
Fixed in **v53.4.0** by commit
[`a76a1920`](https://github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark/commit/a76a1920dc7587be700a17f1592f58a9512ad214)
(PR [#1957](https://github.com/kubeshark/kubeshark/pull/1957)).

In `cmd/mcpRunner.go`: `pod_regex` is now appended **last**, after a
literal `--` end-of-options separator, so it is always parsed as the
`[POD REGEX]` positional and can never be interpreted as a flag. (`namespaces` /
`release_namespace` are passed through `-n` / `-s` value flags, which consume
their value token and are therefore not injectable.)

## Workarounds
- Do not run `kubeshark mcp` with `--allow-destructive` unless required.
- Do not expose the MCP server to untrusted content / untrusted agent inputs.
- Restrict the kubeconfig/permissions available to the machine running the MCP
  server.

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command

cves.summary:
### Impact

Two effects, sharing the root cause of Advisory 1 — header names chosen by the sender were
resolved through Python attribute lookup and rewritten before lookup.

**Uncaught exceptions.** A crafted message raises an exception that is *outside* the
`MailParser*` hierarchy, so a caller catching only mail-parser exceptions does not catch it
and the worker dies.

*Header named after a method* (CWE-248, reported by @iam-niranjan). Python resolves real
class attributes before `__getattr__`, so a header named after a method put a bound method
object into the parsed mail dict. A 12-byte email is sufficient. Nine colliding names were
confirmed: `Parse`, `Message`, `Write_Attachments`, `From_File`, `From_File_Obj`,
`From_File_Msg`, `From_String`, `From_Bytes`, `Get_Server_Ipaddress`. Also reproducible from
the CLI (`mail-parser -f evil.eml -j`).

```python
import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_string("Parse: x\r\n\r\n").mail_json
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type method is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> {"parse": "x", "has_defects": false}
```

*Header carrying 8-bit bytes* (CWE-248). For a header containing raw 8-bit bytes, Python's
`compat32` policy returns an `email.header.Header` rather than a `str`, which the `_raw`
accessor passed straight to `json.dumps`. This fires on entirely benign non-ASCII mail via
`parse_from_bytes()`, the normal entry point for mail off the wire.

```python
import mailparser
mailparser.parse_from_bytes(b"Subject: caf\xe9\r\n\r\nbody\r\n").subject_raw
# 4.6.1 -> TypeError: Object of type Header is not JSON serializable
# 4.6.2 -> '["caf�"]'
```

**Silent loss of message content** (CWE-436). A sender can make a header's value vanish from
every output surface, or be replaced by a different header's value, with `has_defects`
remaining `false`. This is an evasion primitive: the tool's output diverges from the bytes
actually in the message, and a pipeline scanning parsed output for indicators sees nothing
and no failure signal.

Header names were normalised before lookup — underscores folded to dashes, and `_json` /
`_raw` suffixes interpreted — so a header genuinely named `Subject_json` was reported with
the value of `Subject` and its own value discarded, and any header whose name contains an
underscore resolved to nothing.

```python
import mailparser

raw = ("From: Real Sender <real@good.example>\r\n"
       "Subject: innocuous\r\n"
       "Subject_json: MALWARE-C2 http://evil.example/payload.exe\r\n"
       "X_Spam_Flag: YES\r\n\r\nbody\r\n")
mail = mailparser.parse_from_string(raw)
print(mail.mail["subject_json"])       # 4.6.1 -> '"innocuous"'   4.6.2 -> the real value
print(mail.headers["X_Spam_Flag"])     # 4.6.1 -> ''              4.6.2 -> 'YES'
print("MALWARE-C2" in mail.mail_json)  # 4.6.1 -> False           4.6.2 -> True
print(mail.has_defects)                # both  -> False
```

A related case: `email.message.Message.__len__` returns the header count, so a message with
**no headers** is falsy. `parse()` returned before initialising state, and the unset
attributes were then absorbed by `__getattr__` and answered as absent headers. Every
property returned `''` — including `mail` and `attachments`, which are documented to return
a `dict` and a `list` — with no error and no defect flag.

```python
import mailparser
mail = mailparser.parse_from_string("Click http://evil.example/pay.exe now\r\n")
print(repr(mail.body))         # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> the text
print(repr(mail.attachments))  # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> []
print(mail.has_defects)        # 4.6.1 -> ''    4.6.2 -> True
```

### Patches

Fixed in **4.6.2**. Upgrade with `pip install --upgrade mail-parser`.

Header names taken from a message are now looked up literally — no attribute access, no
case or separator folding, no suffix interpretation — so no header name can collide with a
method or property, and no value can be substituted or dropped. 8-bit values are coerced to
`str` before serialisation. Parser state is initialised before the message check, which now
tests `is None`, and attribute names beginning with `_` raise `AttributeError` instead of
being answered as headers.

**Behaviour changes.** Header names now appear in `mail` and `headers` exactly as sent, so a
header named `X_Spam_Flag` keeps that name and its own value. `X_raw` always returns a JSON
array — an absent header yields `[]` where 4.6.1 returned `null`.

### Workarounds

None for the data loss. For the uncaught exceptions, callers who cannot upgrade should wrap
`mail_json`, `mail_partial_json`, `headers_json` and any `X_raw` access in a bare
`except Exception` rather than catching only `MailParserError` subclasses.

cwe.name: Uncaught Exception

cves.summary:
### Patches

Fixed in **4.6.2**. Upgrade with `pip install --upgrade mail-parser`.

Candidate addresses are now selected by position, not by appearance — a bracketed address
the sender wrote is byte-identical to one the MTA wrote, so no amount of pattern matching
can tell them apart:

- the first token of the `from` clause is the HELO name, whatever its shape, and is never a
  candidate;
- an explicit HELO marker inside a comment group is sender text and is excluded;
- a candidate must sit inside a `(` / `[` group;
- IPv4 and IPv6 matches are merged positionally, never family-first;
- the walk stops at the first trusted hop naming no address, rather than continuing into
  sender-written headers.

The IPv6 pattern was corrected to skip the `IPv6:` tag and to prefer the longest valid form.

**Behaviour change.** `get_server_ipaddress()` now returns `None` rather than an unreliable
value in two cases that previously returned an address: a `from` clause consisting of a bare
address with no HELO marker (indistinguishable from `EHLO <that address>`), and a trusted hop
naming no address at all. Callers must handle `None`.

### Workarounds

None within mail-parser. Callers who cannot upgrade should not treat the return value of
`get_server_ipaddress()` as trustworthy, and should derive sender attribution from an
authenticated signal instead — the MTA's own logs, or SPF/DKIM/DMARC results computed
outside this library.

cwe.name: Improper Input Validation

cves.summary:
### Summary

Two regular expressions used while parsing email headers backtrack
polynomially on attacker-controlled input. Parsing a single small, well-formed
email can consume minutes to hours of CPU, denying service to any process that
parses untrusted mail.

Both are reachable from an ordinary `parse_from_string()`, `parse_from_bytes()`
or `parse_from_file()` call — no special API, option, or malformed structure is
required by the victim.

### Details

**1. Address-header fallback regex (`src/mailparser/utils.py`)**

`get_addresses()` falls back to `_ADDR_FALLBACK_RE` whenever
`email.utils.getaddresses(strict=True)` yields no usable address. The
alternative `([^<,]*?)\s*<([^>]+)>` overlaps a lazy quantifier with an adjacent
`\s*` — a space matches both. Driven by `finditer`, which retries at every
offset and rescans the remainder, matching degrades to **quadratic** on `<`
padding and **cubic** on whitespace padding.

The fallback engages on the feature's own happy path, e.g.
`From: alice@example.com <bob@example.com>`.

Measured (4.6.0, CPython 3.14, macOS arm64; reproduced identically on Linux and
on CPython 3.9, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13):

| Padding                | Parse time         |
| ---------------------- | ------------------ |
| valid address + 750 sp | 0.38 s             |
| + 1500 sp              | 2.97 s             |
| + 3000 sp              | 23.4 s (×7.9/2×)   |
| + 6 KB sp              | 185 s              |
| ~100 KB sp             | hours              |

Fully RFC 5322-compliant folded headers (all lines ≤ 71 octets) trigger the same
blowup, so the input passes normal MTA and library checks. ~100 KB of headers is
within Postfix's default `header_size_limit = 102400`.

All six address headers parsed by the library (`From`, `To`, `Cc`, `Bcc`,
`Reply-To`, `Delivered-To`) are affected and their cost adds up linearly.

**2. Received-header clause splitter (`src/mailparser/const.py`)**

`parse_received()` splits on `_CLAUSE_SPLITTER`,
`(?:^|\s+)(from|by|via|with|id|for|envelope-from)\s+`. Under `re.split` this
backtracks **quadratically** over any whitespace run that is not followed by a
clause keyword. The pre-existing normalization collapsed only `[\t\n]`, so
literal spaces — including folded-header padding — reached the splitter intact.

Measured: 24 000 spaces in one `Received:` header → 22 s; ~100 KB → minutes.

### Impact

Availability. A handful of small emails keeps every parsing worker of a mail
gateway, ticketing system, quarantine UI, or archiving pipeline permanently
busy. No confidentiality or integrity impact.

Anyone who parses email they did not author is affected — which is the library's
purpose.

### Patches

Fixed in **4.6.1**.

- The address fallback is now a linear scan: the header is split into
  comma-separated items (quote-aware, in Python), then each item is matched
  against a bounded angle-address `<([^<>\s]+)>` with the display name derived
  in Python, falling back to a bare-email match. Each pattern has a single
  non-nested quantifier over a negated character class → O(n).
  2000 padding spaces: `3.5 s → <0.01 s`. 256 KB padding: `hours → 0.087 s`.
  Output is preserved on every previously supported shape.
- `parse_received()` collapses whitespace runs to a single space before
  splitting, so the splitter's `\s+` only ever matches one character → O(n).
  The date is extracted from the raw header beforehand, so date formatting is
  unaffected. 24 000 spaces: `22 s → 0.003 s`; 200 000 spaces: `0.004 s`.

Regression tests assert linear-time behaviour for both paths.

### Workarounds

None within the library. Upgrade to `4.6.1`.

Users who cannot upgrade immediately should cap total header size before
parsing and enforce a wall-clock timeout around each parse.

cwe.name: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity

cves.summary:
A path traversal vulnerability was identified in mail-parser when extracting email attachments using the write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

A specially crafted email containing malicious attachment filenames (for example, using directory traversal sequences such as "../" or absolute filesystem paths) could cause files to be written outside the intended output directory. Depending on how the library was used and the permissions of the executing process, this could result in arbitrary file overwrite.

The vulnerability affects mail-parser versions 3.8.0 through 4.5.0.

The issue has been addressed by introducing comprehensive filename sanitization and path validation before any file is written to disk. The fix includes:

- Sanitization of attachment filenames before writing.
- Validation that all output paths remain within the intended destination directory.
- Rejection of symbolic link targets.
- Normalization of Windows and POSIX path separators.
- Validation and rejection of invalid or unsafe filenames.
- Protection applied consistently in both write_attachments() and write_sample() APIs.

Users are strongly encouraged to upgrade to the patched release.

## Credits

The vulnerability was responsibly reported by **Niranjan Ganesan** (Security Insights, https://securityinsights.io/, GitHub: @iam-niranjan).

The vulnerability was analyzed, remediated, and the security fix was implemented by **Fedele Mantuano**, maintainer of mail-parser (LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/fmantuano/).

mail-parser would like to thank Niranjan Ganesan for following a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process and for collaborating throughout the remediation and verification of the fix.

cwe.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

cves.summary:
termux-sync restore trusts fields inside an untrusted backup manifest and uses them as the extraction destination without validation.

During restore, each archive entry is handled as:

  src_dir = Path(info.get("source", ...)).parent
  extract_archive(archive, src_dir, ...)

extract_archive opens the archive and runs tarfile.extract for every member with no path jail and no filter:

  with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:*") as tf:
      for member in tf.getmembers():
          tf.extract(member, dest_path, set_attrs=True)

There is no check that manifest "source" stays under an expected restore root, that tar members stay inside dest_path, or that backup_name used in temporary paths cannot contain ".." or separators.

Impact:
A victim who restores a malicious backup (local, shared, or from a compromised GitHub/Google Drive storage backend) can have arbitrary files written anywhere the Termux user can write. Overwriting shell startup files or executable scripts leads to local code execution on later use.

Reproduction (benign markers only):

1. Build a backup directory with home.tar.gz (members: proof filename + optional config names) and manifest.json.
2. Set files.home.source to any path whose parent is the desired write directory (e.g. $HOME/dummy_for_parent so parent is $HOME).
3. Run the same extract path the tool uses: src_dir = Path(source).parent; tarfile.extract each member into src_dir.
4. Observe attacker-controlled files created under $HOME and under other chosen roots (config / shell-rc style overwrite).

Expected: restore only writes under fixed, validated roots; reject unsafe source values and members that resolve outside dest.
Actual: write destination is fully controlled by manifest.source; proof files and overwrites appear outside any intended jail.

Fix direction:
- Do not trust manifest "source" for extract roots; use fixed app-defined destinations
- Sanitize backup_name (basename; reject ".." and separators)
- Extract with tarfile filter="data" (or equivalent boundary checks) and refuse escape
- Treat backups as untrusted input

Actual result (local marker-only reproduction):

PROOF path: /data/data/com.termux/files/home/PWNED_BY_TERMUX_SYNC_RESTORE.txt
PROOF exists? True
PROOF content:
PWNED
This file was written by a malicious termux-sync backup restore path.
Root cause: manifest files.*.source controls extract destination.

*** VULN CONFIRMED: arbitrary write to $HOME ***

important.conf => secret=ATTACKER_CONTROLLED
*** VULN CONFIRMED: overwrite under attacker-chosen root ***

.bashrc_sim shows injected:
export ATTACKER=1
*** VULN CONFIRMED: startup-file style overwrite ***

Extract roots used:
  home  -> parent($HOME/dummy_for_parent) = $HOME
  config -> parent(.../victim_sim/nested_dummy) = .../victim_sim

Reported and credited to Niranj R Mahaswar ( GitHub: @NiranjMahaswar )

cves.summary:
### Impact

`code-review-mcp-server` exposes MCP tools (`getLocalGitDiff`, `codeReview`, `createPR`, `getPRTemplate`) that accept `folderPath` and `baseBranch` string parameters. These caller-controlled values were interpolated directly into shell command strings executed via `child_process.execSync()`, which runs commands through `/bin/sh`.

A crafted value such as `baseBranch = "main; <arbitrary command> #"` (or a `$(...)` command substitution, or a `folderPath` that breaks out of the surrounding quotes) results in **arbitrary command execution** on the host running the MCP server.

### Patches

Fixed in **1.5.3**. Every `execSync()` call was replaced with `execFileSync()` using argument arrays, so inputs are passed directly to `git` / `gh` without going through a shell, eliminating the injection at its root.

### Workarounds

None. Upgrade to `code-review-mcp-server@1.5.3` or later.

cves.summary:
Next.js applications with `'use cache'` can disclose cached data across root params when the same `'use cache'` function is called both directly during rendering and through `unstable_cache()`, and that function reads a root param. Root params are route parameters of the root layout, and applications commonly use them to scope data, for example per locale.

During a cold process start, a cross-request deduplication race allowed an `unstable_cache()` call to join the in-flight fill of a concurrent direct call and receive its result, bypassing the root param check that would normally reject it. `unstable_cache()` then stored that result under a cache key without root params, so subsequent requests for other root param values received the same entry until it is revalidated or evicted. Cached data produced for one root param value is returned to requests for other values.

Exploitation requires the `unstable_cache()` request to arrive while the function's first fill after a process start is still in flight. Outside this race, the nesting already throws an error: `'use cache' inside unstable_cache() is unsupported`, and avoiding it is a complete workaround.

cwe.name: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization

cves.summary:
## Summary

`nltk.parse.dependencygraph.dot2img` invokes the Graphviz `dot` executable without the trusted-execution guarantees that NLTK applies to its other native-tool wrappers. The function resolves `dot` by bare name and then runs the resolved absolute path with a raw `subprocess.run`, omitting the ownership/writability check and the loader-environment scrub that `nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted` provides. On a POSIX host, a local, unprivileged actor who can write to any group/world-writable directory that appears on the victim's `PATH` can plant a trojan `dot`; when the victim later renders a `DependencyGraph` (for example in a Jupyter notebook, which auto-invokes `_repr_svg_`) or calls `dot2img` directly, the planted binary executes as the victim. The advisory GHSA-6hwm-xvph-95vm (CVE-2026-78680) addressed the same untrusted-search-path class for the Graphviz `dot` invoker in `nltk/translate/api.py`, but `dot2img` received only part of that remediation and remains exploitable.

## Root Cause

NLTK's native-tool security model layers four defenses (documented in `nltk/EXTERNAL_TOOL_SECURITY.md`): (1) `find_binary` refuses a current-working-directory-relative match; (2) `resolve_trusted_executable` verifies the resolved file is a regular file that no other unprivileged user can replace (private parent directories, owner is the user or root, no group/world write bit); (3) shell execution is refused; (4) `safe_env` scrubs loader and interpreter environment variables before exec. Layers 2, 3, and 4 are reached only through `nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted`. `dot2img` calls `find_binary("dot")` (layer 1 only), then executes the result with `subprocess.run([dot_binary, ...])` and no `env=` argument. Layer 1 rejects only non-absolute matches, so an absolute path returned by the `which` search stage survives even when the file lives in a writable directory. Because `dot2img` never calls `spawn_trusted`, the ownership check and environment scrub never run.

```text
nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:626   dot_binary = find_binary("dot")          # layer 1 only
nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:631   subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...)   # no trust check, no env=
nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:638   subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...)   # binary-format branch, same gap
nltk/internals.py:1034              if searching_bare_name and not os.path.isabs(path): continue  # skips only relative matches
nltk/translate/api.py:145           process = spawn_trusted(dot_binary, [f"-T{output_format}"], ...)  # hardened sibling
```

## Impact

Prerequisites: a POSIX host on which the attacker is a local, unprivileged user (or code) able to write to a group/world-writable directory that appears on the victim's `PATH`. This includes the commonly cited case of a Homebrew `/usr/local/bin` with `drwxrwxr-x` permissions, or a writable directory placed early on `PATH`. The attacker plants a trojan `dot` there. When the victim renders a `DependencyGraph` (notebook `_repr_svg_` auto-invocation) or calls `dot2img` directly, the trojan executes as the victim, yielding arbitrary local code execution in the victim's account: a local privilege-escalation and lateral-movement primitive. Because the child environment is not scrubbed, loader-injection variables (for example `LD_PRELOAD`, `DYLD_*`, `GCONV_PATH`) also reach the child, providing an additional execution surface. No control over NLTK inputs is required.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires: POSIX host, an importable NLTK build from the affected tree, and Python 3. No third-party dependencies.`

1. Create a world-writable directory and write an executable `dot` script into it that drops a marker and emits fake SVG.
2. Prepend that directory to `PATH` and run from a neutral working directory (so this is not the current-working-directory vector).
3. Show that `resolve_trusted_executable` refuses the planted binary (so the hardened path would raise) while `dot2img` executes it.

```python
import os, stat, tempfile, subprocess, sys
d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
dot = os.path.join(d, "dot")
with open(dot, "w") as f:
    f.write("#!/bin/sh\ntouch " + os.path.join(d, "MARKER") + "\necho '<svg><!-- planted dot ran --></svg>'\n")
os.chmod(dot, 0o777)
os.chmod(d, 0o777)
os.environ["PATH"] = d + os.pathsep + os.environ["PATH"]
os.chdir("/")
from nltk.pathsec import resolve_trusted_executable
from nltk.parse.dependencygraph import dot2img
print("resolve_trusted_executable(planted dot):", resolve_trusted_executable(os.path.join(d, "dot")))
out = dot2img("digraph G { a -> b }")
print("dot2img stdout:", repr(out))
print("planted dot executed (marker created):", os.path.exists(os.path.join(d, "MARKER")))
```

```text
resolve_trusted_executable(planted dot): None
dot2img stdout: '<svg><!-- planted dot ran --></svg>\n'
planted dot executed (marker created): True
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** On a shared POSIX host, a group/world-writable directory is present on the victim's `PATH` (for example a writable directory early on `PATH`, or a Homebrew `/usr/local/bin` with group-write). The attacker writes a trojan `dot` into it.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the contents of the planted `dot` file; no control over NLTK inputs is needed.
3. **Path:** The victim renders a `DependencyGraph` (notebook display triggers `_repr_svg_` at `nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:209`, which calls `dot2img`) or calls `dot2img` directly.
4. **Guard:** `find_binary("dot")` applies layer 1 only (`nltk/internals.py:1034`), which discards a relative current-working-directory match but returns the attacker's absolute path from the `which` stage; `dot2img` never invokes `resolve_trusted_executable` (layer 2) or `safe_env` (layer 4), unlike the hardened sibling `nltk/translate/api.py:145`.
5. **Primitive:** `subprocess.run([dot_binary, "-T%s" % t], ...)` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:631` and `:638`) executes the untrusted absolute path with the full inherited environment.
6. **Result:** Arbitrary local code execution as the victim, plus a loader-injection surface via the unscrubbed environment.

## Bypass Evidence

Canonical prior advisory: GHSA-6hwm-xvph-95vm (CVE-2026-78680), "Uncontrolled search path when invoking the Graphviz 'dot' binary" (CWE-426/CWE-427), patched at `>= 3.10.3`. That remediation was two-part: a uniform layer-1 current-working-directory refusal in `find_binary`, and a routing of native-tool `dot` invocations through `nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted` (layers 2 and 4). Inspection of the current released tree (nltk 3.10.3) shows `dot2img` received the layer-1 change (the function was rewritten from a bare `subprocess.run(["dot", ...])` to `find_binary("dot")` plus a run of the absolute path, with a CWE-426/427 comment at `nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:622-625`) but did NOT receive the `spawn_trusted` routing. The sibling `nltk/translate/api.py:145` does route through `spawn_trusted`, and `nltk/EXTERNAL_TOOL_SECURITY.md` lists Graphviz `dot` only under `translate/api.py`; `dot2img` is absent from the hardened-wrapper inventory. Attempts to invalidate the finding all failed: (a) the claim that the fix covers all `dot` resolution is refuted because layer 1 filters only non-absolute matches and `dot2img` never reaches layers 2/4; (b) the duplicate hypothesis is refuted by a negative control, planting `./dot` in the working directory with none on `PATH` makes `find_binary("dot")` raise `LookupError`, so the prior fix's working-directory guard still fires and this is the distinct residual ownership/environment gap; (c) the "system dot shadows the trojan" objection is refuted because realistic exploitation prepends the writable directory on `PATH` or replaces a `dot` already living in a writable `PATH` directory; (d) both the text and binary format branches share the identical unguarded exec, so it is not format-specific. A fresh PoC on the examined tree confirms `resolve_trusted_executable` refuses the planted binary while `dot2img` executes it.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip (PyPI)`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, latest published release as of the review date; source tree VERSION == 3.10.3)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The `dot2img` function has invoked `dot` via a raw subprocess since well before the prior advisory. The prior advisory's `spawn_trusted` standardization routed only the sibling `translate/api.py` invoker through the trusted-execution chokepoint, so this residual gap in `dot2img` exists from at least that remediation release onward and remains present in the latest published release (3.10.3). Precise introduction and remediation boundaries below 3.10.3 could not be independently established in this environment (no git tags or release history in the checkout); the confirmed statement is that the latest published release is affected and no fix for `dot2img` exists.

## Suggested Fix

Route `dot2img`'s execution through `nltk.pathsec.spawn_trusted(dot_binary, ["-T%s" % t], input=...)`, mirroring the sibling `nltk/translate/api.py`, so that the ownership/writability check (layer 2) and the loader-environment scrub (layer 4) apply, and handle `TrustError`/`OSError` with the same refusal pattern used at `nltk/translate/api.py:152-157`. Apply the change to both the text-format and binary-format branches. Add Graphviz `dot` under `nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py` to the per-wrapper inventory in `nltk/EXTERNAL_TOOL_SECURITY.md` so the second invoker is tracked. Interim mitigation without a code change: ensure no group/world-writable directory appears on the `PATH` of any account that renders NLTK dependency graphs, and install Graphviz in a directory writable only by the user or root.

cves.summary: ### Summary The fix for CVE-2026-46342 (GHSA-g8wj-3cr3-6w7v) binds each `/__nuxt_island/_.json` path to its props by hashing the `(name, props, context, source)` tuple. That hash was computed over `ohash`'s serialization, which does not escape quotes inside strings or delimiters inside keys, so two different prop objects can produce the same hash. A request with crafted props can therefore pass validation for another island's path and render different content at that path. ### Impact For example, these two prop objects serialize identically and share one island path: ```js { html: '', note: '' } { html: '\',note:\'' } ``` This reopens the scenarios described in GHSA-g8wj-3cr3-6w7v: - **`nuxt generate` / prerendering.** Nuxt caches prerendered island responses by path. If the crawler reaches a link to the colliding URL (for example in user-submitted content included in the build) before it renders the page that uses the legitimate props, the colliding response is written into the generated page. - **Path-keyed shared caches.** A CDN or reverse proxy that caches `/__nuxt_island/*` by path only, ignoring the query, can be primed with the colliding response. An attacker has to construct props that collide with a specific legitimate tuple, which in practice means at least part of that tuple is a string they control (for example a stored comment or profile field passed as a prop). Where a prop reaches an unsafe HTML sink in the island (`v-html`, `innerHTML`, a renderer treating a prop as HTML), the substituted response can execute script in the site's origin. Without such a sink, the impact is content substitution. Applications are not affected if they do not use server components or ``, or if no island receives attacker-influenced string props. Server-rendered responses that are not cached by path alone are also unaffected. ### Patches Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.4` and `@nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.4`. The island hash is now computed over a canonical JSON encoding of the tuple, in which strings and keys are escaped, so different props can no longer produce the same hash. Island hashes change as a result. Clients that build island URLs themselves should use the exported `getIslandHash` rather than hashing with `ohash` directly. Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to Nuxt 4. ### Workarounds - Ensure any intermediary cache keys `/__nuxt_island/*` on the full query string, not on the path alone. - Treat island props as untrusted input and do not pass them to `v-html` or other HTML sinks without sanitisation. - When prerendering, avoid including user-submitted links to `/__nuxt_island/` in crawled pages, for example by excluding that prefix with `nitro.prerender.ignore`: ```ts export default defineNuxtConfig({ nitro: { prerender: { ignore: [route => route.startsWith('/__nuxt_island/') && route.includes('?')], }, }, }) ``` ### Credits Thanks to rat5ak for reporting this issue.

cves.summary:
### Summary

When using the webpack or rspack builder, the dev server serves built client chunks to any request whose `Host` header matches its `Origin`/`Referer`, or that carries `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`. After a DNS rebinding attack both headers name the attacker's hostname, so a malicious page opened while `nuxt dev` is running can read `/_nuxt/*.js` and exfiltrate the app's source. This bypasses the same-origin check added for [GHSA-4gf7-ff8x-hq99](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-4gf7-ff8x-hq99), [GHSA-6m52-m754-pw2g](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-6m52-m754-pw2g) and [GHSA-x6qj-4h56-5rj5](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-x6qj-4h56-5rj5).

### Impact

A developer runs `nuxt dev` with `builder: 'webpack'` or `builder: 'rspack'` (the default config is enough; `--host` is not required) and opens a page on an attacker-controlled hostname, for example `http://rebind.attacker.example:3000/`. The attacker then re-points that hostname at `127.0.0.1`. Requests from the page now reach the dev server as same-origin requests:

```bash
curl -H 'Host: rebind.attacker.example:3000' -H 'Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin' http://127.0.0.1:3000/_nuxt/app.js
# 200, with the compiled modules
```

The page can read the response with `fetch`, which exposes the compiled source and its inline source maps, module identifiers, the developer's local filesystem paths, and any developer-controlled values inlined into the client bundle (for example through a custom `DefinePlugin`). With rspack, the HMR websocket also accepts connections from the rebound hostname. Private `runtimeConfig` is not part of the client bundle.

The attacker needs to know or guess the dev server port and to time the DNS change. Chrome 142+ and other Chromium-based browsers that enforce [Local Network Access restrictions](https://developer.chrome.com/release-notes/142#local_network_access_restrictions) prompt before a public page can reach a loopback address.

The default Vite builder is not affected: Vite rejects unknown `Host` headers through `server.allowedHosts`. Production builds are not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in `@nuxt/webpack-builder` 4.6.4 and `@nuxt/rspack-builder` 4.6.4. The dev middleware now rejects requests whose `Host` header is not `localhost`, `*.localhost`, an IP address, or a hostname allowed by the new `devServer.allowedHosts` option or by `vite.server.allowedHosts`, before any `Sec-Fetch-Site`/`Origin`/`Referer` checks. This includes `devServer.host` and the hosts `nuxt dev` allows for the addresses it listens on; `nuxt dev --public` allows any host, as it does with Vite. With rspack, the same list is passed to rsbuild's `server.allowedHosts`, which covers the HMR websocket.

When accessing the dev server through another hostname, for example through a reverse proxy, add that hostname to `devServer.allowedHosts` (a leading `.` also allows subdomains; true allows any host).

Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix.

### Workarounds 

- Use the default Vite builder for development.
- Use Chrome 142+ or another Chromium-based browser that enforces Local Network Access restrictions, and don't open untrusted sites in other browsers while the dev server is running.
- Treat secrets inlined into the client bundle during development as exposed and rotate them.

### Credits

Nuxt thanks Anthropic for reporting this through coordinated disclosure (ANT-2026-VKRM97G5).

cves.summary:
### Summary

Nuxt matches route rules against the request path with encoded slashes (`%2F`) left encoded, while the page router decodes them into route params. A request that spells a slash as `%2F` can therefore render a page through a catch-all route without the route rules configured for the path it resolves to. The fix for [GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp) deliberately left reserved escapes such as `%2F` encoded, so it did not cover this form.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass route rules that protect paths served by a catch-all page route, or by a custom route whose param can span several segments.

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/docs/internal/**': { appMiddleware: 'auth', headers: { 'X-Frame-Options': 'DENY' } },
    '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' },
  },
})
```

With `app/pages/docs/[...slug].vue`, `/docs/internal/guide` runs `auth`, but `/docs/internal%2Fguide` renders the same page without running `auth` and without the header. With a root `app/pages/[...slug].vue`, `/admin%2Fsecret` is rendered instead of redirected.

The rules skipped include server-side `redirect`, `headers`, `proxy`, `ssr` and `noScripts`, and `appMiddleware`, `appLayout` and `redirect` as matched in the app during server rendering and client navigation. `getRouteRules` returns the same incomplete result.

Whether the page then shows protected content depends on how it reads the route:

- With a route such as `definePageMeta({ path: '/docs/:path(.*)' })`, `route.params.path` is `internal/guide` for both requests.
- With a repeatable catch-all (`[...slug].vue`), `route.params.slug` is `['internal/guide']` instead of `['internal', 'guide']`, so a page that joins the segments (`slug.join('/')`) to load content loads the protected resource.
- `route.path` keeps the encoding (`/docs/internal%2Fguide`), so a page that loads content by `route.path` does not resolve it.

Not affected:

- Static page routes and params that match a single segment. `/docs%2Finternal` does not match `app/pages/docs/internal.vue`.
- API handlers in `server/api` and `server/routes`. As far as we can tell, Nitro matches these against the same path as its route rules, so a handler and the rules for it agree.

Browsers send `%2F` in a path as written, so a plain link is enough to reach the page.

### Patches

Fixed in `nuxt@4.6.4`, together with `@nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.4` and `@nuxt/vite-server@4.6.4`, which it depends on. Route rules are now resolved for both the request path and the path with each `%2F` read as a separator, and the rules matched by either apply. Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix.

### Workarounds

Reject page requests whose path contains an encoded slash in a server middleware:

```ts
// server/middleware/encoded-slash.ts
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  if (/%2f/i.test(event.path.split('?')[0])) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 404 })
  }
})
```

This also rejects legitimate uses, such as an API route that takes a scoped package name (`@scope%2Fname`) as a param; narrow the check to the path prefixes your route rules protect if you need those.

A reverse proxy or CDN that rejects or decodes encoded slashes before forwarding the request also removes the mismatch.

### Credits

Thanks to Riahi Foudhil for reporting this issue.

cves.summary:
### Summary

`Application.add_domain()` compiled each `*` in a host mask to `[^:]*`. With two or more wildcards in a mask, matching a long `Host` header that does not match the mask took polynomial time on the event loop.

### Impact

An attacker could stall a server that registers a domain mask with more than one wildcard by sending requests with a long `Host` header.

### Workaround

Use at most one `*` in a domain mask.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/c6ac0e44c3c573ff9616f4a6a532992538b31e43

cves.summary:
### Summary

`Set-Cookie` parsing created additional cookies from unrecognised `name=value` attributes, and `CookieJar` had no limit on the number of cookies stored or sent. A server could make the client store a very large number of cookies and generate very large `Cookie` headers.

### Impact

A malicious server could cause excessive memory and CPU use in a client, repeated on every redirect, and cause later requests to the same domain to build an excessively large `Cookie` header.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/6963ee0befec1502b6bb7b4db6c72d044c08f4fa

cves.summary:
### Summary

`Request.post()` had no limit on the number of fields in a URL-encoded form body. Inserting a large number of repeated keys into a `MultiDict` took quadratic time on the event loop.

### Impact

An attacker could block the event loop with a form POST within the default `client_max_size` to any handler that calls `Request.post()`.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/615fec3d4f088f30d2ee72cad760152e92aa1c53

cwe.name: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity

cves.summary:
### Summary

When reading a multipart part with `Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64`, `BodyPartReader.read_chunk()` kept reading until the chunk length was a multiple of 4, with no byte limit. A part with a short `Content-Length`, or a long run of whitespace, could cause the entire remaining body to be read into memory within a single call before any size check, or spin on the event loop.

### Impact

An attacker could bypass `client_max_size` to cause excessive memory use, or block the event loop, with a specially crafted multipart request to any handler that reads multipart data.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/a555ab698e08e9baea7386d5b4c0761cb8956fdd

cwe.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption

cves.summary:
### Summary

The `max_msg_size` check in the WebSocket reader added the declared frame length to the size of the partial message already buffered. In the C extension this addition is 64-bit arithmetic, so a declared length close to 2**63 overflowed and the check passed.

### Impact

An attacker could bypass `max_msg_size` and cause unbounded memory use by streaming an oversized WebSocket message after a small non-final fragment.

### Workaround

If unable to upgrade, the Python reader is unaffected and can be used with `AIOHTTP_NO_EXTENSIONS=1`.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/8cfbe9abe5e11b84006a10f9bdf82bf607671dab

cwe.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

cves.summary:
### Summary

While a request flagged as an upgrade (e.g. a WebSocket handshake) was being handled, all further data received on the connection was buffered with no size limit or flow control until the handler completed.

### Impact

An attacker could cause unbounded memory use by streaming data behind an upgrade request to any handler that does not immediately accept or reject the upgrade.

Patch: https://github.com/aio-libs/aiohttp/commit/3d850ee9b92573c7e913821cbcb96005beb3f4df

cves.summary:
### Impact

Shiny for Python's bookmark-restore path accepted a client-supplied `_state_id_`
query-string value and joined it into the server-side bookmark directory
(`<cwd>/shiny_bookmarks/<id>`) without validating it. A value containing `..`
path segments, or an absolute path, could therefore cause the server to open and
parse `input.json` and `values.json` from a directory outside the bookmark store.

On a default application the restore was attempted whenever the client supplied a
URL query string — including when bookmarking was disabled
(`bookmark_store="disable"`) — so no opt-in configuration was required. For such
applications the impact is an unauthenticated, server-side probe for the
existence and JSON-validity of attacker-chosen paths, constrained to those two
file names.

Applications configured with `bookmark_store="server"` **and** using
`ui.input_file()` are affected more seriously. The file-input restore handler
copies files out of the restore directory, so the contents of an
attacker-selected file name within an attacker-selected directory could be read
into the application.

### Affected versions

1.4.0 through 1.6.3. Bookmarking was introduced in 1.4.0; earlier releases do
not contain the affected code path and are not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in **1.6.4**. Upgrade with:

```
pip install --upgrade shiny
```

The fix validates bookmark IDs against an allowlist — a single path segment
matching `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`, which cannot express a path separator, a `..` parent
reference, or an absolute path — before the ID is used to build a filesystem
path. Bookmark IDs generated by Shiny are unaffected by this restriction.
Restore is additionally gated on the application's `bookmark_store` setting at a
single point, so it no longer runs when bookmarking is disabled, and the on-disk
restore path is honored only under `bookmark_store="server"`.

### Workarounds

There is no configuration change that mitigates this on an affected version:
the restore path ran even with `bookmark_store="disable"`. Deployments that
cannot upgrade immediately can strip the `_state_id_` parameter from incoming
query strings at a reverse proxy or load balancer, which prevents the affected
code path from being reached.

### Credits

Reported by [@0xRenSec](https://github.com/0xRenSec).

cves.summary: A Windows NT log file has an inappropriate maximum size or retention period.
A Windows NT account policy does not forcibly disconnect remote users from the server when their logon hours expire.
A network intrusion detection system (IDS) does not properly handle packets that are sent out of order, allowing an attacker to escape detection.
A network intrusion detection system (IDS) does not properly handle packets with improper sequence numbers.
A network intrusion detection system (IDS) does not verify the checksum on a packet.

Buffer overflow in the search component for iPlanet Web Server (iWS) 4.1 and Sun ONE Web Server 6.0 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a long argument to the NS-rel-doc-name parameter.

The pfexec function for Sun Solaris 8 and 9 does not properly handle when a custom profile contains an invalid entry in the exec_attr database, which may allow local users with custom rights profiles to execute profile commands with additional privileges.

The Lithtech engine, as used in (1) Contract Jack 1.1 and earlier, (2) No one lives forever 2 1.3 and earlier, (3) Tron 2.0 1.042 and earlier, (4) F.E.A.R. (First Encounter Assault and Recon), and possibly other games, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (connection refused) via a UDP packet that causes recvfrom to generate a return code that causes the listening loop to exit, as demonstrated using zero byte packets or packets between 8193 and 12280 bytes, which result in conditions that are not "Operation would block."

Winamp 5.07 and possibly other versions, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash or CPU consumption) via (1) an mp4 or m4a playlist file that contains invalid tag data or (2) an invalid .nsv or .nsa file.
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in UseModWiki 1.0 allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via an argument to wiki.pl.

Cross-site scripting vulnerability in fom.cgi of Faq-O-Matic 2.712 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary Javascript on other clients via the cmd parameter, which causes the script to be inserted into an error message.
